name: Medicine
description: How medicine learned to heal: vaccines, anaesthesia, antibiotics, transplants and the reading of the human genome.

checkpoints.name: Early medicine
checkpoints.note: For thousands of years healers drilled skulls, bled patients and used herbs, from Chinese needles to Andean bark. Hippocrates and Galen shaped Greek and Roman medicine, Vesalius mapped the body and Harvey the blood, and Leeuwenhoek saw tiny life in the 1670s, but no one knew that germs caused disease.

checkpoints.name: Vaccines, germs and anaesthesia
checkpoints.note: Jenner showed that cowpox prevents smallpox, anaesthesia let surgeons work slowly, and Nightingale reformed nursing. Pasteur and Koch built the germ theory, which showed that germs cause disease. X-rays and aspirin arrived at the end of the century.

checkpoints.name: Antibiotics and insulin
checkpoints.note: Insulin and penicillin turned deadly illnesses into treatable ones, and machines such as the iron lung and the kidney dialyser kept patients alive. Some fashionable treatments, such as lobotomy, later proved tragic mistakes.

checkpoints.name: Transplants, scanners and the pill
checkpoints.note: Polio vaccines emptied the wards, pacemakers and transplants repaired hearts, scanners looked inside the body, and the pill and IVF changed family life. The thalidomide disaster led to tougher drug testing.

checkpoints.name: Genes and new vaccines
checkpoints.note: Medicine turned to genes and information. The Human Genome Project read human DNA, gene editing with CRISPR promised cures for inherited disease, and mRNA vaccines were designed and approved within a year to fight a new virus in 2020.
